name: Mian
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: [p.98] There are no consistent stress patterns in Mian. However, syllables which are assigned H or HL from any of the tonal melodies H, HL, or LHL are more prominent that syllables which are assigned L. The phonetic manifestations are that they are longer and have high or falling pitch, e.g.: sékú [sɛ́ˑkʰúˑ] 'bushknife' ... Words with L tone are pronounced with no conspicuous change in pitch, e.g.: ibal [ìβàl] 'dust' ... [p.70] Both nominals and verbs are lexically specified for one tonal melody and an accent which indicates where the tonal melody is to be inserted. ... Generally, the accent for all stems is placed on the last stem syllable. Both nominals and verbs show accent placement which deviates form this rule.
new_statements.citation: Fedden, Sebastian Olcher. 2007. A Grammar of Mian, a Papuan Language of New Guinea. PhD thesis, University of Melbourne.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.8.10 'Tone and syllable prominence', p. 98 (PDF p. 99); supporting: sec. 2.8.2 p. 70 (PDF 71), sec. 2.5.3 p. 57 (PDF 58), sec. 1.3 p. 25
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mian is a word-tone language: each word carries one of five tonemes (L, H, LH, LHL, HL) anchored at a lexically specified 'accent' that by default sits on the last stem syllable (initial syllable if it contains pharyngealized /aˤ/; verbs are unaccented, stem-accented, or off-stem-accented, the last shifting the anchor one syllable right under suffixation). There is no independent stress system: perceived prominence (extra length, high/falling pitch) simply falls on whichever syllables receive H or HL from the melody, and all-L words have no prominent syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; prominence is a by-product of tone, not a metrical system.
new_statements.exceptions: Nominals with pharyngealized /aˤ/ in the first syllable take initial accent (kaˤwá 'steel axe', p.57, 78); off-stem-accented verbs shift the accent to the syllable after the stem when suffixed or auxiliary-compounded (p.70, 93); Future suffixes /aˈmab/, /oˈmab/ are inherently accented (p.95); benefactive applicative /b/ makes unaccented verbs stem-accented with LHL (p.96); unaccented (all-L) verbs 'do not have a prominent syllable' (p.90).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of tone/accent assignment is the phonological word including affixes and most clitics; nominal and verbal compounds count as one phonological word with one melody and one accent (p.25). Statements concern citation/word forms; vowel length also varies with syllable count (monosyllable > accented syllable of disyllable > of trisyllable, p.53-54).
new_statements.identity_note: Fedden's description is explicitly based on the eastern dialect (East Mianmin, villages around Mianmin airstrip, Gubil, Fiak, Hotmin; thesis p. 28: 'The language description presented in this thesis is based on the eastern dialect') = Glottolog mian1256 (dialect mian1257 'Mianmin'). The western variety (West Mianmin / Wagarabai / Suganga, around Yapsiei) is a separate Glottolog languoid suga1249 [sug] and is not the object of the description.

sources.note: Mian is a word-tone language (5 tonemes L, H, LH, LHL, HL assigned to the phonological word) with a lexically specified accent = anchor point for the melody, by default on the last stem syllable (p.70; p.57), initial if first syllable has pharyngealized /a/; verbs unaccented / stem-accented / off-stem-accented. Sec. 2.8.10 (p.98): 'There are no consistent stress patterns in Mian'; H/HL-toned syllables are more prominent (longer, high/falling pitch); all-L words have no prominent syllable.
